disclosure: Fully synthetic account-discovery examples, not customer research. These standalone practices are not linked to the 500 sales opportunities and do not change pipeline totals. Reported needs and baselines are invented; software fit and real-world outcomes are unvalidated.

examples.name: Practice A
examples.systems: Generic practice-management system plus a spreadsheet follow-up list; no vendor affiliation.
examples.workflow: Staff copy claim follow-up items into a spreadsheet, check the payer portal, then re-enter status in the practice-management system.
examples.reportedNeed: The fictional billing lead reports duplicate status entry and difficulty keeping the follow-up list current. The work log illustrates time spent, not avoidable cost or proven savings.
examples.baseline: March 16–20, 2026: 60 claim follow-up items, 300 staff minutes in the invented work log. No implementation or before/after result is recorded.
examples.payerContext: Medicare and commercial payers are mentioned in the fictional notes; payer shares, denial rates and collection delays are unknown.
examples.openQuestions: Can the current system already manage this queue? What share of work is duplicate entry, and which payer or denial categories drive it? Obtain a longer baseline and confirm the workflow with its owner.
examples.reviewer: RCM solutions consultant with the practice billing lead (illustrative roles)
examples.nextCheck: Walk through one de-identified follow-up task and compare the fictional work log with current-system capabilities before assessing software fit.
examples.decision: Request a billing-workflow review; software fit remains pending.

sources.content: Billing lead: We use a spreadsheet beside the PM system. Staff copy follow-up items out, check payer portals and type the status back in. Keeping both lists current is difficult. Medicare and commercial payers are in the mix; shares and denial rates were not supplied.
Period: March 16–20, 2026. Claim follow-up items: 60. Staff minutes: 300. Time by activity, payer, denial reason and recoverable dollars: not supplied.

examples.name: Practice B
examples.systems: Generic practice-management system with an existing follow-up queue; no vendor affiliation.
examples.workflow: Staff work the existing queue and record status in the same system. The supplied fictional note reports no separate spreadsheet or duplicate entry.
examples.reportedNeed: The fictional administrator reports no current follow-up workflow complaint. This limited note cannot establish overall billing performance or rule out other needs.
examples.baseline: March 16–20, 2026: 60 claim follow-up items, 45 staff minutes in the invented queue excerpt. This is a separate practice, not an improvement over Practice A or evidence of vendor performance.
examples.payerContext: Medicare and commercial payers are mentioned in the fictional notes; payer shares, denial rates and collection delays are unknown.
examples.openQuestions: Do the billing team and a longer reporting period support the administrator's account? What explains the payment comparison? Payer mix, denials and collection performance remain unknown.
examples.reviewer: Account analyst with the practice administrator (illustrative roles)
examples.nextCheck: Record that no billing-workflow need was identified in these fictional records. Ask the billing owner to confirm the current process before considering any recommendation.
examples.decision: No billing-workflow need identified in the supplied fictional records; no software recommendation.

sources.content: Practice administrator: Staff use the PM follow-up queue and update status there. We do not maintain a separate spreadsheet, and I have no current complaint about this workflow. Medicare and commercial payers are in the mix; shares and denial rates were not supplied. Billing-team confirmation is pending.
Period: March 16–20, 2026. Claim follow-up items: 60. Staff minutes: 45. Payer mix, denial rates and collection performance: not supplied.
